articles.title: SonicWall CVE-2026-19868: A Valid Password That Skips SAML and Your MFA
articles.excerpt: SonicWall CVE-2026-19868: A Valid Password That Skips SAML and Your MFA Bit4Bit DFIR, practical notes for people who actually run the systems. If your SonicWall firewall sends SSL VPN logins through S…
articles.body: SonicWall CVE-2026-19868: A Valid Password That Skips SAML and Your MFA Bit4Bit DFIR, practical notes for people who actually run the systems. If your SonicWall firewall sends SSL VPN logins through SAML so your identity provider can enforce multi-factor authentication, patch it now. CVE-2026-19868 lets someone who holds valid credentials for a different login method on the same firewall skip the SAML step, and with it the MFA prompt. This is not an unauthenticated remote code execution bug. It is narrower than that, and in some ways worse: it defeats the exact control most teams point to when they say remote access is protected by MFA.

articles.title: Offline-First, Zero Backend: Building a Tailoring Business App That Works Without Internet
articles.excerpt: Every tailor I know keeps his whole business in paper registers. One notebook for measurements. Another one for orders. Payments live in a third place, which is mostly his memory. It works, right up u…
articles.body: Every tailor I know keeps his whole business in paper registers. One notebook for measurements. Another one for orders. Payments live in a third place, which is mostly his memory. It works, right up until the busy season, when the pages fill with arrows and crossings-out and one regular customer's sizes end up in the margin of a book from two years ago. TailorVexa is the app I built to replace those registers. It runs a tailoring shop from the phone in the tailor's pocket: customer profiles, measurements, orders and payments, all in one place. And the decision I made before writing a single screen still shapes everything about it: No internet required. No account. No server. Everything stays on the phone.

A production agent needs an answer to harder questions: who can invoke it, what can it remember, which actions require review, how do you trace a bad decision, and what happens when a model call stalls? AWS's November 11 reference architecture for Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is interesting less because it makes Java agents autonomous, and more because it treats those questions as part of the application. The post by Viquar Khan and Mahammadali Saheb walks through a travel assistant and a document-processing system, with a runtime contract, tool calling, memory, rules, human review, resilience, and observability.[1] This is a reading of AWS's published design and sample, not a hands-on deployment or benchmark.

articles.body: What a complete non-coder in Japan learned building, launching, and charging for a real product using only prompts — and an AI partner. I am not an engineer. Before this project, I had never built an app, never written production code, and honestly, never expected to ship anything that strangers could pay for. In November 2026, I launched my first product anyway. It's called Ippin Log — a food log that doesn't record restaurants with stars, but records a single dish by its taste . Not "this place was 4.2 stars." But: light vs. rich, thin noodles vs. thick noodles, crisp vs. chewy. Every genre — ramen, curry, and seven others — gets its own two-axis taste chart. Over time, your logs become a map of your own palate.

articles.title: Linear Light Upscaling Is Correct, and It Cost Me 18 Shadow Levels
articles.excerpt: Every resampling article opens with the same demo: downscale a black-and-white checkerboard in sRGB, get a muddy grey that should have been mid-grey, then do it in linear light and get the right answe…
articles.body: Every resampling article opens with the same demo: downscale a black-and-white checkerboard in sRGB, get a muddy grey that should have been mid-grey, then do it in linear light and get the right answer. The demo is correct. I have reproduced it. Then I took that conclusion — "always resample in linear light" — and applied it to a real 512×512 photograph, and to a shadow gradient, and to an unsharp mask. It is not that simple, and the reasons are specific enough to measure. Seven experiments below. Two of them contradict the advice I started with. All of them run on numpy 1.26.4 and Pillow 12.2.0, and every number comes from the snippet at the end. Why the theory says linear light wins sRGB is a non-linear encoding. A stored value of 128 is not 50% of the light — it is about 21%.

articles.title: Cross-validation, and the split that hides a model's failure
articles.excerpt: Cross-validation is how most models get their score. Six points worked through by hand show how k-fold works, and how the same model scores 0.80 or −0.67 depending only on how the data was split. A mo…
articles.body: Cross-validation is how most models get their score. Six points worked through by hand show how k-fold works, and how the same model scores 0.80 or −0.67 depending only on how the data was split. A model has to be scored on data it was not trained on, or the score only measures memory. Holding back one test set works, but with little data the score then depends heavily on which rows landed in it. Cross-validation fixes that by testing on every row exactly once. It also has a failure that does not show in the number. I ran into it in my research, which I wrote about in a note on a model that scored perfectly . This note works both parts through by hand. How k-fold cross-validation works Split the data into k equal parts, called folds. Train on k − 1 of them and test on the one left out.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: The first day of my career was October 1, 2002. I’d been lucky enough to get hired by Official Xbox Magazine. The fledgling Xbox console was not quite a year old, and when I got settled in on the staff, it quickly became clear that Xbox was really about one thing above all else: Halo. I remember being surprised in my first days on the job by what would happen every single day, like clockwork, at 5pm: consoles and TVs would get turned on, Halo would get fired up, and we’d all play a round or two of Capture the Flag on Blood Gulch before we all went home. Fun and friendly banter ensued. Halo was baked into the Xbox’s DNA from the very start. It is one of my very first of many thousands of great Xbox memories.

articles.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
articles.excerpt: "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."
articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. articles.excerpt: After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15's booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its "Mechazilla" launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed 'chopst…
articles.body: After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15's booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its "Mechazilla" launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ' chopstick ' catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company's third-quarter earnings call that "success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight." articles.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
articles.excerpt: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Hele…
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely .
